what: Commvault sells software that backs up company data and puts it back after something goes wrong. Its newer products are aimed specifically at ransomware: proving a clean copy exists, testing that it restores, and rebuilding an environment after an attack. Most of it is now sold as a subscription or as a managed cloud service called Metallic.
customers: IT and security teams at mid-sized and large organisations, plus government agencies and regulated industries that must prove they can recover data.
money: Term licences and the Metallic cloud service, billed annually and renewing.
Older perpetual licences, maintenance contracts and professional services.
moat: Backup software is bought once and trusted for a decade. It sits beneath every application, the recovery procedures are written around it, and the staff are certified on it, so replacing it is a project nobody volunteers for. Commvault also covers an unusually wide range of systems, which matters to large organisations whose estates include decades of accumulated technology.
risks: The shares trade at about 79 times earnings and 52 times EV/EBITDA. Net income is only $82.7M because of heavy share-based compensation and the transition to subscription billing.
Rubrik and Cohesity were built for the cloud era and have taken the newer accounts, which is where the growth is.
Veeam dominates the mid-market and competes on price, which limits what Commvault can charge below the enterprise tier.
Microsoft, Amazon and the storage vendors each bundle backup functions into their own platforms, which erodes the reason to buy a specialist at the simpler end.
Seventeen analysts average a $189.38 target, about 24% above the current price, which is a modest margin for a stock on this multiple.
opportunities: Revenue has grown every year shown, from $769.6M in 2022 to $1.2B in 2026, and the growth has accelerated rather than slowed.
Free cash flow of $255.7M is three times reported net income, because subscriptions are paid upfront and the accounting charges are largely non-cash.
Cash of $900.0M against $36.6M of debt is an exceptionally clean balance sheet.
Ransomware has turned backup from an IT housekeeping cost into a board-level requirement, which has changed both the buyer and the budget.
The shift from perpetual licences to subscriptions depresses reported revenue and profit while it happens and flatters both once it is done.
watch: Annual recurring revenue growth and net retention. Reported earnings are distorted by the subscription transition and by stock compensation; the recurring revenue base is the only clean measure of whether the business is winning.
view: Commvault spent most of the 2010s as the example people used when they wanted to describe a legacy software company being overtaken. Veeam took the mid-market, Rubrik and Cohesity raised enormous sums and took the cloud-native accounts, and Commvault’s growth stalled in the single digits with a perpetual-licence model that was going out of fashion. What has happened since is a genuine turnaround, and the market has noticed: revenue has gone from $770 million to $1.2 billion, growth has accelerated rather than decayed, and three-quarters of revenue now recurs.

The reason it worked is worth understanding, because it tells you how durable it is. Ransomware changed who buys backup software and why. It used to be an insurance policy bought by an IT manager on a tight budget; it is now a board-level requirement with a security budget behind it, and the question has shifted from ’can you store a copy’ to ’can you prove the copy is clean and that it restores’. That reframing suited Commvault, which already covered the sprawling mixture of old and new systems that large organisations actually run, better than it suited the newer vendors optimised for cloud-first estates.

Now the valuation. At 79 times earnings the stock looks absurd, and on reported earnings it is — but reported earnings are the wrong measure here for two specific reasons. Free cash flow is $256 million against $83 million of net income, a three-to-one ratio, because subscription customers pay upfront while the accounting recognises revenue over time, and because a large slice of the cost line is share-based compensation that consumes no cash. On free cash flow the multiple is about 24 times, with $900 million of net cash on the balance sheet. That is a demanding price for a software company growing in the high teens, but it is not a ridiculous one, and the gap between 79 and 24 is the single most important thing to understand before forming a view.

Where I would be careful is competitive rather than financial. Commvault has won the recovery and resilience argument in the enterprise, but the long-run pressure in this category is bundling: Microsoft, Amazon and the storage vendors all have reasons to include adequate backup for free, and ’adequate’ is usually enough below the enterprise tier. Commvault’s defence is that proving recoverability across a messy estate is genuinely hard and that nobody rips out backup software casually — both true, and both the kind of moat that holds for a long time and then does not. I would own this on recurring revenue growth and net retention and ignore the earnings line entirely until the subscription transition finishes washing through it.
bull: Ransomware keeps backup in the security budget, recurring revenue compounds in the high teens, and the market eventually values the business on its free cash flow rather than its depressed earnings.
bear: Bundled backup from the cloud and storage vendors erodes the base from below while Rubrik and Cohesity take the new accounts, leaving a high multiple on decelerating growth.
